TechnologyTab.title: Could tech replace firefighters in the battle against wildfires?
TechnologyTab.text:
The pictures are familiar, terrifying fires being tackled by firefighters and planes dropping water.

Hundreds of thousands of people have been forced to leave their homes across France, Spain and Portugal as wildfires tore through forests and countryside.

In France, four men have already lost their lives fighting the wildfires and another 150 have been injured.

But why are humans and 30-year old planes being used? Why can drones replace soldiers in Ukraine but not firefighters?

Chief sergeant Guillaume Millet, a firefighter of 24 years experience heads the Fire and Rescue Service branch of the CFDT union in the Gironde, the region worst hit by wildfires in France this summer.

He says that while the techniques for tackling fire have not changed much, technology in forest fire detection has.

"The big change, especially in my département, is that now we've got cameras assisted by artificial intelligence to watch the forest and see where fires are starting," Millet says.

"In the Gironde, cameras have replaced the human look-outs we had in watch towers in every town throughout the summer months," he says. Those lookouts were often students.

The switch has reduced false alarms, he says. "An AI-assisted camera can distinguish with almost total certainty between smoke and dust thrown up by a tractor in a field, for example."

They have an impressive range as well, detecting fires up to 20km (12 miles) away.

In the Gironde, the system was installed by a company called Midgard. In other parts of France, it's another French start-up called FireTracking.

"As soon as the system detects a fire, there's an alert on the fire fighters' telephones. They open the application and see what the camera is seeing with a x40 [40 times] zoom," explains FireTracking's CEO Jean-Simon Chaudier.

"Next to that real-time video there's a map with the exact location of the fire, the position of any nearby houses and a simulation of how, given the weather, the level of humidity and so on, it is expected to spread from minute to minute," he adds.

And every minute is vital. "For the past 10 days, for example, we have the feedback from a firefighter that our AI detected seven fires 15 minutes before the first phone call. If you can help a firefighter to save 15 minutes, it's the difference between a catastrophe and a fire which can be limited to two or three hectares," Chaudier says.

"After one minute you can put out a fire with a glass of water, after two you need a tank of water, after three minutes you need to send a Canadair," Chaudier says, talking about the amphibious planes that scoop up water from rivers, lakes and the sea to dump it on the flames that are the spearhead of forest fire fighting here and around the world.

FireTracking's cameras are currently surveying a million hectares, mainly in France.

The cost? In the French département of Indre-et-Loire, the company has installed 11 detection sites.

"In all €1.2m [$1.4m; £1m] was spent to cover the whole 6,000 sq km area [2,300 sq miles]," says Chaudier.

It is mainly agricultural land. Crop fires are a huge and expensive problem with some 300 a year in this département alone, Chaudier says.

AI fire detection is going to get better over the coming years. The French civil protection service has a programme called Condor, for example, which is testing solar-powered drones that carry out continuous patrols with electro-optical cameras and AI.

There are also projects with sensors placed among the trees. Spain's SenForFire, for example, which measures gases released before flames become visible.

As for drones, firefighter Guillaume Millet says they're being tested in France for sea rescue, dropping lifebuoys and survival kits, but there's no drone tech that's reached that stage yet for firefighting.

"In fact, the usefulness of technology is very limited in this area," Millet says. "It can help us with detection but it's not technology that puts out fires; you need people to pull the hoses through the forest to attack them."

Not even aircraft can replace that, he says.

"When a Canadair drops 6,000 litres of water on a wildfire it reduces its intensity but then firefighters on the ground have to finish what the Canadair started."

The French are also getting used to the sight of Dash planes that spray fire retardant (ammonium phosphate in the form of an orange powder) in front of the flames to prevent the vegetation from catching fire too quickly.

But again, that's no substitute for the brawn and water brought by troops on the ground.

Not yet, at least.

A French start-up called Daidelos is trying to raise investment for a heavy-lifting, petrol-engine drone.

If it gets off the ground, it will be able to hover over a fire, spraying it with 1.2 tonnes of water.

Companies are also developing drones that drop grenades which explode when they come in contact with extreme heat, covering the surrounding area with a chemical powder that smothers, cools and interrupts the combustion chemistry of the fire.

The hope here is that this could form an autonomous first response, so forest fire detection and drone activation can be so quick that fires can be extinguished as they're starting. It would not be able to do anything against a wildfire once it's really got going.

French researchers are also working on drones that could fly close to the flames. That wouldn't be to fight the fire exactly but to seize vital information about it; to assess the risks – smoke, sudden weather changes, collapse of burning trees or buildings - before the firefighters move in.

Technology is already helping firefighters detect fires faster and react to them more effectively. It might soon be able to make their job less dangerous. But replacing them is unlikely, according to Gironde firefighter Guillame Millet.

"It's always the firefighters on the ground, pulling the hoses, who extinguish the fires," he says. This has been the case since the creation of the first modern fire brigade in the Netherlands in the 1670s. It is not about to change soon.

TechnologyTab.title: Apple issues new challenge against UK order for access to private user data
TechnologyTab.text:
Apple has confirmed it has launched a new legal complaint against the UK government at a court that deals with objections to the use of covert surveillance powers.

The tech giant has not told BBC News what the complaint relates to but the Financial Times, external has reported it is another challenge to a Home Office demand for so-called "backdoor" access to highly encrypted Apple user data.

The row, which centres on the government's desire to be able to see material protected by an advanced data protection system - which currently even Apple itself cannot access - has been rumbling on since early 2025.

The government said it would not comment on legal proceedings or what it called "operational matters".

But it added in a statement: "The UK supports strong encryption and robust privacy protections, but it is also vital that law enforcement can access communications when necessary and proportionate to protect the public from terrorism, serious crime, and child sexual abuse."

Apple has meanwhile referred reporters to a statement given last year, after its initial challenge to the UK government's request.

This said it was "gravely disappointed" it could still not offer its Advanced Data Protection feature to new UK users, following its decision to withdraw it in February 2025.

"As we have said many times before, we have never built a backdoor or master key to any of our products or services and we never will," the company added.

Advanced Data Protection is an opt-in feature that allows users to turn on a higher level of protection for data stored in iCloud, such as back-ups, Drive storage, photos and voice memos.

It is secured using end-to-end encryption - meaning not even Apple would be able to see its contents.

The government's requests for Apple to permit it access to data held under this system were issued under the Investigatory Powers Act (IPA).

It includes powers allowing the government to issue secret notices - called technical capability notices - which can secretly force companies to provide UK security services with ways to access customer data.

The government had fought unsuccessfully to keep legal challenges to its first notice to Apple secret.

Its notice was later withdrawn after angering US politicians, who were concerned it would affect their own citizen's data.

But the government issued a new request in October which did not apply to US users.

Privacy groups which previously campaigned against its secret orders welcomed Apple's new legal complaint.

"We are happy to learn that Apple is once again challenging the UK's regime of secret orders," said Privacy International.

"While we don't know the substance of Apple's claim, if it relates to the previously reported orders aimed at undermining the security of Apple's iCloud storage, then Apple's claim, alongside side ours and Liberty's, is crucially important to preserving all of our privacy and security."

Ruth Ehrlich, director of external relations at Liberty, said the case was "hugely important" and has "far-reaching implications for the public's privacy rights well into the future".

"End-to-end encryption is an essential security tool that protects our personal data, including our bank details, health information, private conversations and images," she said.

"Opening a backdoor to all of that information carries a wide range of risks to our personal data. It is critical that the Government listens to the many concerns and commits to protecting our privacy rights."

But Sir Brian Leveson, the Investigatory Powers Commissioner, who provides independent oversight of the use of surveillance powers, has previously criticised media use of the term "backdoor", external.

He said notices such as those concerned in this case would only be issued "if the Secretary of State deems it necessary and proportionate, and this decision is independently reviewed and approved by a Judicial Commissioner".

He added requests for data would also require separate authorisation under the IPA and these would be subject to independent oversight.

TechnologyTab.title: ‘Mamma mia!’: Trump tariffs refund ignites 53% profit spike at Nintendo
TechnologyTab.text:
Nintendo has reported a jump in profits, as the Japanese game maker’s earnings were buoyed up by a long-awaited refund on Donald Trump’s tariffs.

The company said profits surged 53.5% to ¥147.4bn (£694m) over the three months to June, substantially beating expert forecasts for ¥77.8bn.

Nintendo said sales of its Switch 2 console, which was released last summer, “maintained strong sales momentum”, while popular games such as Yoshi and the Mysterious Book, Star Fox, and Pokémon Pokopia “performed steadily”. However, that did not make up for an overall drop in sales compared with the same period last year, with revenue down by 10% to ¥517.8bn.

Instead, Nintendo said profits were aided by a refund on US tariffs, after the country’s supreme court ruled in February that Donald Trump’s sweeping “liberation day” trade levies were illegal.

The Trump administration has refunded about $100bn from the tariffs charged before the court ruling, representing 60% of the total $165bn collected. Trump has continued to pitch tariffs as a solution for the US economy, bringing back domestic production, securing better trade deals and closing the deficit in the federal budget.

Nintendo’s Tokyo-listed shares were up 2.87% on Thursday after the earnings release.

The company filed a lawsuit weeks after the US supreme court ruling, demanding a full refund from the White House that would cover what it spent on tariffs, plus interest.

While a refund now appears to have come through, Nintendo stopped short of confirming the full amount, at a time when it is still appears to be resisting calls to pass those refunds on to consumers.

Last month, Nintendo was hit with a class action lawsuit on behalf of customers, which claims the company hiked its prices because of tariffs but later benefited from the refunds. Nintendo’s lawyers described the lawsuit as “meritless”, and that the price customers paid represented “the purchase price of the goods they wanted and received.”

TechnologyTab.title: Rising number of UK children report seeing explicit deepfakes of themselves
TechnologyTab.text:
Children in the UK have reported a surge in explicit deepfake images featuring their likenesses, as a safety watchdog warned AI is making such content easier to produce.

The Report Remove service, which blocks intimate images from appearing online, said there had been a rapid increase in imagery that had been digitally manipulated or “faked” in some way, including with AI and nudification tools.

In the first six months of this year it received 420 reports from children of images of themselves that they believed had been faked or manipulated to appear explicit. The number has already exceeded its 2025 total of 397.

Dan Sexton, chief technology officer at the Internet Watch Foundation (IWF), which operates Report Remove alongside the NSPCC children’s charity, said the figures underscored the difficulty of preventing online images from being manipulated in an age of widely available and capable AI tools.

“If someone can take a benign image of a child from the internet and create child sexual abuse material with it, there is nothing that child can do to stop it from happening apart from preventing anyone from taking pictures of them – or not putting pictures of themselves online,” he said.

Report Remove has received so many reports of manipulated images from under-18s in recent years that it has added a check box to its online submission form allowing them to flag the material as deepfaked.

Sexton said the figures confirmed a fear that AI would improve in capability and be used to manipulate images of real people.

“This is one of the harms we were worried about when we first saw AI image generators being used, that they would be used to create child sexual abuse material featuring real children,” he said.

“Everyone in the world is at risk,” Sexton added.

The IWF, which monitors the distribution of child sexual abuse material [CSAM] online, said the majority of the reports of manipulated images made to Report Remove in 2025 and 2026 were so severe that they passed the CSAM threshold. AI-generated CSAM is illegal in the UK and the government has made it illegal to adapt an AI model to create abuse material or to distribute such models to others.

Rani Govender, an online safety expert at the NSPCC, said tech companies must put stronger safety protections in their AI products to prevent the creation of explicit material.

“This rise in children reaching out because fake or AI‑generated sexual images have been created of them is alarming but also sadly predictable,” she said. “Tech companies cannot keep pushing out AI products without embedding strong protections that prevent this material from being created in the first place.”

Sexton said some victims who had contacted Report Remove about manipulated images had been targeted for sextortion, where a blackmailer threatens to publish the material unless they receive financial payment or demands more explicit images from the victim.

Report Remove is a service that allows children to anonymously flag intimate images or videos of themselves that have been sent to former partners, sextortion fraudsters or could appear online. The service turns those images into a “hash”, or digital fingerprint, which is shared with major tech platforms, which can take the image down or prevent it from being uploaded.

The rise of AI-enabled deepfakes has prompted a series of warnings about posting identifiable pictures of children online.

Last month the National Crime Agency and IWF encouraged parents and guardians to keep pictures of their children away from public display online. They suggested making social media accounts private or sharing pictures of children through a “close friends” group only.

The guidance also followed cases in which cybercriminals had attempted to blackmail schools by scraping pictures of children, using AI to convert them into child sexual abuse material, then threatening to publish the imagery. Schools have been urged to remove identifiable pictures of pupils’ faces from their websites and social media accounts.

TechnologyTab.title: Google DeepMind enters a new era as co-founder Demis Hassabis shifts AI role
TechnologyTab.text:
When Sir Demis Hassabis said AI had brought the world to a “pivotal moment in human history” last month, he knew another big change was imminent.

This shift was closer to home. The Nobel prize-winning head of Google DeepMind, Google’s AI unit, announced this week he was relinquishing his day-to-day duties as chief executive and becoming chair. He is also taking on the role of chief scientist at DeepMind’s parent, Alphabet.

Hassabis and DeepMind have been key players in AI’s breakthrough era. The 50-year-old co-founded DeepMind and sold it to Google in 2014, which gave him the resources to oversee a number of advances.

These included building the AlphaGo system that mastered the Chinese board game Go and developing AlphaFold, a programme that predicts the 3D structure of proteins. The latter resulted in Hassabis being jointly awarded the 2024 Nobel prize in chemistry.

A former Google executive said the leadership overhaul showed London-based DeepMind being brought firmly into the orbit of its parent in Mountain View, California. DeepMind will now be run by Hassabis’s longstanding colleague, the US-based Koray Kavukcuoglu, who will take the non-CEO role of senior vice-president of DeepMind.

“The era of DeepMind as an independent actor is over and the obvious sign of that is you have gone from a charismatic founder-leader to appointing Koray in a non-CEO leadership role. Koray is a technical character, not an inspirational figure like Demis,” said the former executive.

The ex-Google employee added that it would be “galling” for Google and Hassabis that the latest iterations of Google’s flagship AI model series, Gemini, have lost ground to rival models developed by its US rivals Anthropic and OpenAI.

Hassabis has said he was looking forward to focusing more on the “big picture” for AI and believed he was handing over operational management of a unit that was well placed for the competitive battles ahead.

Internally, DeepMind is a workplace where there have been political tensions. Employees who spoke to the Guardian said there was internal disquiet over the company’s work with the Pentagon. Earlier this year, a former Google DeepMind employee launched a legal challenge against Google, claiming they were unfairly dismissed for their views on Gaza.

That employee was involved in unionisation efforts at Google DeepMind, which have taken place against a backdrop of concern that Google’s AI could assist militaries, including the Israel Defense Forces. Another Google DeepMind employee resigned from the company in mid-July, citing Google’s work with the Pentagon and the US Department of Homeland Security.

One said to the Guardian that Hassabis’s departure was the “end of an era”.

“Now the person we were supposed to trust to get the right outcomes for humanity has stepped away,” they said. Google DeepMind “has become just another subdivision of Google”, they added.

Rosa Curling, the executive director of Foxglove, a campaign group that supported the Google DeepMind employee in their legal challenge, said: “The departure of the co-founder of a company that once prided itself on its ethical credentials is likely to cause further concern among its frontier AI staff about how their work will end up being used in the real world.”

Google has said it is committed to the “private and public sector consensus” that AI should not be used for domestic mass surveillance or autonomous weaponry without “appropriate human oversight”. While Google has declined a voluntary union recognition agreement in London, it has said it valued “the constructive and direct dialogue that we have with our employees about building a positive and successful workplace”.

On the commercial side, a new cutting-edge model, Gemini 3.5 Pro, has yet to be released amid reports it has been delayed owing to attempts to improve its code-writing abilities – a core part of the appeal of Anthropic and OpenAI’s best products.

Google’s two AI labs, London-based DeepMind and California-based Google Brain, were merged into Google DeepMind under Hassabis’s leadership three years ago. Control now appears to be moving back to the US, where Google’s co-founder Sergey Brin is reportedly playing a bigger role in AI development.

Citing the departure of the leading AI researcher Yann LeCun from Meta and Geoffrey Hinton from Google as another example of “the end of an era in the AI ecosystem”, the former executive added: “This is very clearly a sign that the science-driven agenda of leadership in these labs has given way to cold, hard commercial reality that all of these companies want to make a return on the hundreds of billions of dollars they have invested in AI.”

The source added, however, that Google still had the benefit of being able to combine its Gemini models with an impressive suite of products, from its all-conquering search product to its cloud platform and YouTube. Thanks to its search business it also has the money to continue investing heavily in AI, having generated net income – a US measure of profit – of $132bn (£98bn) last year.

Hassabis has also taken on a more statesman-like role in recent years. The reference to a “pivotal moment” came in a blogpost in which he called for a US safety body to assess cutting-edge models, with the hope it would lead to the establishment of global standards.

The need for such a body, Hassabis argued, was pressing because the tech industry was approaching the “pivotal” point of achieving AGI, the term for a theoretical state of AI where a system can perform any human cognitive task – which also means being capable of performing white collar jobs in sectors such as law, finance and health.

A Google spokesperson said: “This is a move Demis has been thinking about for a while. He is very excited, and this will give him more time to focus on AI-driven scientific breakthroughs.” They disputed that the changes had anything to do with the performance of Gemini.

Hassabis’s move was announced alongside the departure of Jeff Dean, a veteran Google engineer and DeepMind’s chief scientist, who is leaving along with three other top researchers to form an AI startup called Discovery Loop.

According to one former Google employee, Dean’s departure could augur further personnel losses. Dean’s move also follows OpenAI’s poaching in June of Google’s Noam Shazeer, a leading figure in the field as co-author of the 2017 research paper Attention is All You Need, a crucial step in developing chatbots.

“It’s hugely problematic for Google,” said Jeremy Nixon, a former AI researcher at Google and founder of Infinity Artificial Intelligence Institute, a startup. “It’s problematic because of who Jeff will hire and because the primary reason people want to work at Google is because of him and Noam Shazeer and all these other phenomenal researchers. It’s no longer true to say that if you want to work with the greatest researchers on the planet, you go to Google DeepMind.”

Nixon added that Dean was an “angelic diplomat” who could “deal with these complex political organisations”.

Google denies it faces a post-Dean talent crisis, pointing to attrition rates for AI talent for the first half of this year being lower than they were at this time last year.

If AI is indeed facing a pivotal moment, Google has just had one.

TechnologyTab.title: This man was secretly snapped by someone with smartglasses. He’s not alone in calling that a violation of privacy
TechnologyTab.text:
One summer day earlier this year, Rhys left a cafe in Melbourne where he had been working remotely, when his phone pinged with a message on the dating app Grindr.

The message was a photo of him sitting at a table outside the cafe on his laptop, with his dog seated on the ground next to him. In the foreground, in a man’s hand was an iPhone unlocked.

The photo had been taken moments before with Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses, unbeknown to Rhys.

“He essentially wrote something about my dog being cute and apologised for not saying hi,” says Rhys, who asked that his surname not be used.

Rhys never noticed a flash, despite Meta Ray-Bans requiring an LED light to alert others to the device filming or taking pictures.

It felt creepy, Rhys says, particularly because the person didn’t say hi in the first place before surreptitiously taking a photo to send to him.

Smartglasses, such as Meta’s Ray-Bans, which have built-in cameras, microphones, and AI assistants, are growing in popularity as the clunky, ugly designs of earlier models are replaced with styles that are increasingly indistinguishable from regular glasses.

Meta says it has sold more than 7m of the glasses worldwide. It recruited the celebrity Kylie Jenner to star in online advertisements and partnered with social media influencers across the globe to attempt to bring the technology into the mainstream – and particularly into the hands of women.

Other companies like Snapchat are following with their own versions as tech companies look to find the next evolution beyond the smartphone.

But there is a growing backlash to, as they have been dubbed by some, “pervert glasses”. There are reports of women being filmed without their consent and having their interactions with a glasses-wearing influencer posted on social media. An ad by activist group Everyone Hates Elon features the late sex trafficker and paedophile Jeffrey Epstein wearing the glasses with the slogan “glasses for people who don’t do consent”.

While the price point remains high for the top-of-the-line models, cheaper versions are also becoming popular. Online retailers Amazon and Temu both sell knockoffs, while Australian low-cost retailer Kmart’s Anko-branded $89 camera glasses have already sold out, as Guardian Australia reported this week.

That news led to a petition by Australian activist group GetUp calling for a ban on the Anko glasses. As of Friday it had 21,000 signatures.

“It could be interpreted as a democratisation of access to these technologies,” Dr Fareed Kaviani, a research fellow in the Emerging Technologies Research Lab at Monash University, says of the Anko-branded glasses.

“But it’s not really a democratisation of consent – there’s a total lack of the ability for people to not only know if they’re being filmed … but there’s an inability to consent to being filmed.

“It really changes the dynamics of public space, raises a lot of privacy concerns, and a lot of concerns around the more vulnerable members of the public – especially children.”

Researchers at the University of Sydney analysed 350 publicly-available Instagram videos shot on smartglasses from around the world during 2023 to 2026, showing what they said was “a shift to discreet, point-of-view recording that is difficult for bystanders to detect”.

In a subset of these videos, around 60% of interactions could be classified as potential harassment, with subjects visibly uneasy or attempting to disengage, they say. In 43% of videos women were also abused in the comments of the post with some even revealing their personal details.

“Smart glasses have given pickup artists a new tool to further exploit women,” one of the researchers, Dr Joanne Gray, says in a statement accompanying the early findings on Friday. “You don’t know if you’re being filmed; that footage is then uploaded, exposing you to a wider web of harassment.”

Life-changing vision aid

But smartglasses do have some positive use cases. Graeme Innes, who has been blind since birth, says Meta’s Ray-Bans have been life-changing.

“I just use them all the time, and the fact they’re hands-free, it just makes a huge difference to my everyday life,” he says.

The former disability commissioner, now chancellor of Central Queensland University, says the glasses allow him to go for a walk and get feedback on his surroundings with the help of a visual description service.

At home, he can use it to check his credit card numbers, read a packet on an item in the kitchen cupboard, and to get cooking instructions.

“I was in a restaurant with my wife the other day, and I picked up the menu on the table, and just read it and chose what I want … that’s just something I’ve not been able to easily do in the past,” Innes says.

Chris Edwards, Vision Australia’s chief mission officer, says his life fundamentally changed when he got the Meta Ray-Bans two years ago, with the main benefit being the devices are hands-free, meaning he can use the AI assistant, or visual description services, to navigate.

“Getting support by humans is costly and impractical,” he says. “I do a lot of travelling for my work. And if I wanted to get similar support by a human, I would probably have to hire them for two hours.

“When I’m travelling [now] I can go to a location, put on my Meta glasses and be able to get descriptions of what’s around me, whether it’s a sign or a street sign or a bit about my location, all of those sorts of things.”

Specialist glasses for blind or low-vision people were available prior to the release of the current wave of smartglasses, but Edwards says they cost thousands of dollars and were not covered by the national disability insurance scheme.

Both Innes and Edwards acknowledge privacy concerns, but Innes says “that horse bolted 15 years ago when we got smartphones”.

“You can discreetly take pictures with a smartphone and the same privacy issues are there, so to single out the glasses as problematic – I don’t follow that logic,” he says.

Kaviani says the glasses are a “gamechanger” as an assistive technology, but “they’re not being marketed that way”.

Gray says governments should be acting early before the risks of the technology become “normalised and widespread”, and current privacy and harassment frameworks are not designed to address covert, continuous recording in public and semi-public spaces.

Meta last month rolled out an update that disables the camera if the LED light is interfered with, and also reportedly began removing videos from its platforms of wearers using the device to harass strangers in public.

However, legal recourse can be difficult. A new privacy tort in Australian federal law allows individuals to sue for invasion of privacy, but it is expensive for one person to take on.

If the images are posted to social media, they can be reported under eSafety’s adult cyber abuse scheme or children’s cyberbullying scheme. A spokesperson for eSafety says so far there have been a “small number of complaints where camera-enabled smart glasses may have been involved” and the regulator is closely monitoring how the technologies are being used.

“When it comes to filming people in public, just because technology makes something possible doesn’t necessarily mean it’s appropriate,” the spokesperson says.

The Australian privacy commissioner, Carly Kind, says smartglasses will “fundamentally alter our experience of interpersonal interactions”, and regulators should consider if new laws are required.

“As long as public trust in technology companies remains extremely low, the bar for establishing a social licence for rolling out new tech will be high,” Kind says.

EntertainmentTab.title: Zainab Jiwa: My viral moment with Zendaya at The Odyssey premiere
EntertainmentTab.text:
"I can't zip this! Mummm?"

This was 29-year-old Zainab Jiwa, calling out for help squeezing into a corset while filming a "get-ready-with-me" TikTok video. It's a scene many 20-somethings still living at home will relate to.

The difference is, Zainab was on her way to the recent London premiere of The Odyssey, one of the summer's biggest blockbusters.

She was invited there as a guest and says she caught the eye of Hollywood megastar Zendaya, thanks to her custom look: a striking gold gown complete with a hood.

"She just walked past, and she saw me there. Her jaw just dropped, so did mine," Zainab tells me.

"It was just a stare-off for a minute, and she was like, 'Oh my god, amazing, amazing,' and then she just walked off."

"I’m still in shock,” she adds. “The thought of her noticing my outfit blew my mind."

The interaction went viral, external with 19m TikTok views. Her phone blew up.

While Zendaya has been ruling the red carpets with high-fashion "method dressing" – where stars match outfits to a film's themes – Zainab is perhaps proving that independent creators like her can give Hollywood a run for its money.

Zainab, who is Muslim and wears a hijab, is also often one of the only people covering her hair at premieres, but she says finding ways to incorporate modest wear is part of the fun.

"Even though you're covered, you can still find a way to be on theme.”

Arriving for our interview at BBC Broadcasting House this week, her look was on-point in an olive shirt, tie, and brooches. "I put in effort today," she says.

She's a self-confessed fashion addict. "From the womb," she says, when I ask her when her passion started.

Her other love is film - but she initially kept that as a hobby. Still, she posted videos on social media for fun about her favourite films and outfits inspired by them.

Soon, major studios took notice. Disney was first, offering her a junket interview for the series Moon Knight, where she got to interview stars on the red carpet.

"I thought it was a scam,” she says. “I can’t watch that back. I was NOT good.”

Today, Zainab is a full-time creator and presenter, interviewing A-listers like Denzel Washington, Paul Mescal and Tom Hiddleston – while decked head to toe in outfits paying homage to the films.

She's one of many digital content creators on the red carpet, with others including Chicken Shop Date’s Amelia Dimoldenberg, Reece Feldman and social media personality Jake Shane.

It's not always easy. Sometimes, Zainab gets invites to premieres the night before, meaning a mad rush to sort her look before travelling to the event - often by public transport (“and I look ridiculous”).

She works with a range of designers and brands, but says she also keeps costs down by reusing items as much as possible.

Her outfits are purposely bold, allowing her to "break the ice" with stars. For House of the Dragon season two, she wore a red gown by a student designer featuring three faces wearing hijabs.

"I'm a bit extra, but I like to add culture in everything I do," she says.

For Spider-Man: Brand New Day, she customised her look with spiderweb henna. For Gladiator II, she wore gold armour.

She admits she has worried whether dressing modestly will make it harder for her to succeed in this industry, but she finds pleasure in it too.

"I have a fun time working around the fact that I cover my hair or I cover my arms," she says. "I'd call it halalify the look. I'd always say, ‘'but how do I halalify this?'"

"I enjoy that bit the most because it shows there's no restriction really here."

But while Zainab spends much of her time rubbing shoulders with Hollywood royalty, home life in Harrow, north-west London is completely different.

"Oh my god, my house is chaos," she laughs. Storage space is at a premium, and outfits often end up "shoved somewhere".

She has a cat, siblings who often pop in, and parents who are frequently enlisted for wardrobe emergencies.

Despite it not being the career trajectory they’d expected for their daughter, Zainab says her parents are now "so supportive".

EntertainmentTab.title: Disney agrees deal to let TikTokers use its characters in videos
EntertainmentTab.text:
Disney and TikTok have agreed a deal which will allow creators to use clips from Disney films, including its subsidiaries, in their videos.

It means clips from hit franchises like Star Wars, Toy Story and the Marvel Cinematic Universe will soon start popping up in videos - which will also be shared on Disney's short-form video platform, Verts.

The scheme will be launched in the US before being rolled out to other countries.

Neither company shared financial details of the agreement, although it follows the collapse of a $1bn (£745m) deal between Disney and OpenAI which would have let people use its characters in AI-generated videos.

That agreement was cancelled in March when OpenAI shut down its AI video generation tool Sora, citing a decision to focus on other parts of its business.

"Today, fans are celebrating our stories in entirely new ways," said Disney's chief marketing and brand officer Asad Ayaz, following the TikTok deal being announced.

"Disney owns some of the world's biggest franchises but ownership of attention is shifting towards creators," social media expert Matt Navarra told BBC News.

"Hollywood used to market at fans - now it needs to give fans the raw materials to market with it, and that is quite a profound shift."

TikTok said its platform saw an average of 6.5 million posts relating to film and TV per day last year.

Fans like to use clips from films and TV shows in their videos, but without express permission, they would often be taken down due to copyright claims.

This makes it harder for a wide audience to engage with fan-created content around a big release.

TikTok would also benefit from the "credibility of becoming a formal distribution partner to one of Hollywood's biggest studios," Navarra said.

He added that TikTok's recommendation algorithm gives it the power to "influence which character or scene or forgotten franchise suddenly becomes very valuable again".

Disney and TikTok said a jointly-run programme would boost some creators' videos and give them access to exclusive events.

"This is a deal that repositions and recovers Disney in the UGC [user-generated content] space following the content gap left by the sudden collapse of Sora," Gareth Sutcliffe from Enders Analysis said.

But he said it was not without risk.

"There is an ongoing safety debate around TikTok under European online rules," he said.

"At a minimum, Disney will need to employ significant guardrails to curate the creator content that is selected."

Online creators and influencers are becoming more important to brands' marketing strategies.

Last year, a report from Oxford Economics said YouTube content creators contributed £2.2bn to the UK economy in 2024 and supported 45,000 jobs.

There is also a recognition that even very small influencers, who focus on niche topics, might have lower follower counts but come with a hyper-engaged audience.

Disney launched its short form video platform Verts in the US in March, with plans to expand that further around the world.

EntertainmentTab.title: William Orbit: Madonna and Blur producer dies aged 69
EntertainmentTab.text:
Acclaimed British music producer William Orbit, known for his work with acts including Madonna, Blur, All Saints and Pink, has died at the age of 69.

A statement, external released on Friday by Orbit's family and friends "with profound sadness" said he died at home on 23 July. No cause of death was given.

"He will be greatly missed by us and by so many whose lives he touched through his music, friendship and kindness," the statement said.

London-born Orbit, who real name was William Wainwright, helped to reinvigorate Madonna's career in 1998 with the album Ray of Light, which blended electronic dance music and ambient techno with pop and trip-hop.

It went on to win three Grammy Awards and remains, for many people, the Queen of Pop's greatest record.

Spice Girl Mel C paid tribute, posting that it had been "such an honour to have worked with this great man" on her 1999 debut solo album Northern Star

"Sending all my love," she added.

Nicole Appleton of girl group All Saints wrote, external: "We were fortunate enough to work with him on many occasions and on many songs. In the studio, he made me feel so confident, comfortable and always brought the best out in me.

"He was a treasure in the music industry and we had the most amazing times in the studio and socially. We will forever celebrate him as a music icon. Sending love to all his friends and family."

Skunk Anansie frontwoman Skin noted: "Been dancing to his music for literally decades, thank you for all the great music we shall have forever."

Sister Bliss from fellow London dance act Faithless wrote: "Genius and pioneer... wouldn't have a life in music without him."

Modern electro-pop artist Georgia added: "It was an honour to work with William, I will cherish it forever, long may he live with the electronic acid sounds in the sky."

Speaking to the Official Chart company, external in 2015 about the process of making Ray of Light, Orbit said: "We got in studio, broke all the rules and didn't really think about the consequences.

"I'm very proud of my work on that record - I think it still holds up today," added the musician and composer.

Madonna and Orbit combined again to great effect in 1999 on her number two UK chart hit Beautiful Stranger, which he co-wrote and played on.

The track, which earned them another Grammy, also featured on the soundtrack to the second Austin Powers movie, The Spy Who Shagged Me.

In 2000, Orbit worked on Madonna's album Music, and they reunited in 2012 when he produced six tracks on her MDNA album.

With Blur, Orbit produced the 1999 album 13, which saw the Britpop band take a darker and rawer lyrical turn, providing hit singles such as Tender, Coffee & TV and No Distance Left To Run.

He later worked on their track Sweet Song from 2003's Think Tank album.

Orbit's collaboration with pop star Pink, Feel Good Time, from the soundtrack of 2003 film Charlie's Angels: Full Throttle, brought more success, reaching number three in the UK and bagging another Grammy nomination.

His signature soundscape gave many of his recordings a dreamy, blissful aura - whether on upbeat hits by Madonna or Pink, or slower songs like Pure Shores and Black Coffee by All Saints.

Group member Shaznay Lewis and Orbit wrote Pure Shores for the 2000 film The Beach, starring Leonardo DiCaprio, and the track went to number one in the UK.

Lewis posted a broken heart emoji in response to the news of his death.

His other collaborators included Beth Orton, including co-writing her 1996 single She Cries Your Name; and U2, producing the Irish band's 2002 single Electrical Storm.

Orbit released 12 studio albums as a solo artist, the best-received being Pieces in a Modern Style, which featured his interpretations of various classical pieces.

The album reached number two in 2000, and a dance remix of his version of Samuel Barber's Adagio for Strings was a club smash and went to number four in the singles chart.

EntertainmentTab.title: Jared Leto: Campaigners call for concerts to be cancelled
EntertainmentTab.text:
Warning: Contains graphic details of alleged sexual offences and misconduct, as well as strong language

Women's safety campaigners are calling for Thirty Seconds to Mars' upcoming concerts in the UK to be cancelled after frontman Jared Leto was accused of criminal sexual conduct.

A BBC investigation published last week heard from four women who have accused the US musician and actor of behaviour which includes sexual assault and grooming.

The alleged offences took place in the 2000s and 2010s when the women were teenagers and Leto was in his 30s and 40s. He is now 54.

The musician - who strongly denies the claims - is currently scheduled to perform with his band at two of the UK's biggest arenas next April.

The End Violence Against Women coalition and domestic abuse charity Women's Aid have told BBC Newsbeat they have concerns about the upcoming events in London and Manchester - urging organisers not to go ahead with them.

BBC Newsbeat has contacted the promoters, venues and the band for comment, but has not received any responses.

A spokesperson for Women's Aid told Newsbeat it is "troubling to hear that UK concerts are still planned to go ahead that will put an alleged abuser in the spotlight".

"In light of the very serious allegations of criminal sexual conduct, we would urge organisers to put safety over profit and avoid platforming figures like this."

Janaya Walker, interim director of the End Violence Against Women Coalition, said she backed the charity's call.

"I think it really is about putting people over profit in this instance, and particularly women and girls' safety," she said.

Walker said tickets still being sold for Thirty Seconds to Mars' upcoming concerts at London's The O2 and Manchester Co-Op Live was "really worrying".

"Particularly for victims and survivors of violence against women and girls, they'll be seeing these reports and then seeing that things are moving forward seemingly without any consequence," she said.

"I think that will cause a huge amount of alarm and frustration and anger."

Walker said the coalition wants the industry to consider whether platforming groups and individuals "sends a message" about whether they "condone particular forms of behaviour".

"And that's the choice that I think is in front of them."

US rock band Thirty Seconds to Mars, known for hit songs including The Kill, This is War and Kings And Queens, was formed by Leto and his brother Shannon in the late 1990s.

They began touring in the 2000s and progressed to headlining major arenas around the world.

As part of the BBC documentary Jared Leto: Hollywood's Dark Secret, two men who worked with Leto's band for many years recall how uncomfortable staff felt about the way Leto would interact with teenage girls.

One alleges that crew members were instructed to invite young girls backstage after they would join Leto on stage at gigs.

Another says at one point there would typically be about two girls a day stopping by to see Leto at a house where the band was working.

Among those who have accused Leto is ex-model Alex, who says her agency was invited to a Thirty Seconds to Mars' concert at London's O2 arena in 2013.

She says she was later invited to an after-party by Leto's female assistant and, although she was 19 at the time, she says to protect herself she "felt the need" to pretend to be younger when she met Leto.

She says she told him she was 17, and that Leto, then 41, replied: "Age is just a number, and anyway, we're in Europe."

Alex says one of Leto's assistants encouraged her to go to another party at a nearby hotel later, but only Leto was in the room when she arrived.

When she asked Leto if she could sleep on the chaise longue in the room, Alex says the star responded by saying that, if she did, she would wake up "with a dick in her ass".

Alex says she tried to dismiss what happened, but she now believes the hotel encounter had been "all planned out".

In total, 10 women have spoken to the BBC documentary, with nine of them sharing their stories publicly for the first time.

Despite repeated attempts to contact Jared Leto before publication of the original story, he did not respond to the allegations put to him by the BBC.

After the story was published, Leto said in a statement released by his representatives to the BBC: "I have never sexually assaulted anyone in my entire life. These claims are absolutely and categorically false".

EntertainmentTab.title: Lauryn Hill and Wyclef Jean 'in an amazing place' as fans hope for new Fugees album after 30 years
EntertainmentTab.text:
Lauryn Hill and Wyclef Jean have raised hopes of the Fugees making their first new album in nearly three decades, with Hill saying the band have gone through "an incredible healing process".

The group have not released a studio album since The Score in 1996, which was one of the defining albums of its generation, featuring the hits Ready or Not, Fu-Gee-La and Killing Me Softly.

The pair have reunited on stage a number of times in recent years and spoke to BBC News ahead of a major concert in Milton Keynes on Friday to mark the album's 30th anniversary.

Jean said they are "in an amazing place", and broke into song during the interview to celebrate that he is "back with my bandmate".

The renewed bond between the two was evident during the interview. When asked about the possibility of a new album, Jean began by restating the question, "Will there be music in the future?", and Hill chimed in: "Absolutely."

Jean continued: "All I can tell you is, man, we're in God's hands,” before singing: “I’m back with my bandmate!

"So we're in an amazing place. I think the energy is very important."

He suggested they would continue "projecting that love" to the world.

Hill added: "There was an incredible healing process that happened with us as a band and as bandmates, and as you said we just want to showcase that and give some of that energy to the world as well."

The comments will fuel hopes of a full Fugees reunion, although neither artist confirmed that a new album is currently being recorded.

The group's third member, Pras Michel, is currently serving a prison sentence in the United States following his conviction in a federal lobbying and fraud case.

Hill and Jean were speaking ahead of Diaspora Calling! By Ms. Lauryn Hill, a one-day festival that will make its UK debut at the Milton Keynes National Bowl on Friday.

The event will feature performances from Hill, Jean, Erykah Badu, Giggs, Fireboy DML, YG Marley and Zion Marley, with comedian Dave Chappelle hosting.

Reflecting on the anniversary of The Score, Jean said the Fugees' ambitions had always extended beyond music.

"I remember saying from a very young age, we're not going to do music, we're going to be a movement," he said.

He said the themes explored by the group three decades ago remain as relevant as ever.

"When you talk about the idea of refugees, look where we are today. We were saying these things 30 years ago. It was never just about us – it was always about the movement."

Hill said the Fugees themselves embodied the idea behind Diaspora Calling.

"Our different places of origin came together to unite culture, reflect culture and show people how beautiful, powerful and resourceful that culture is," she said.

Earlier in the day, Hill and Jean surprised fans with a pop-up appearance in London's Piccadilly Circus, performing an a cappella rendition of Ready or Not.

Hill said London was the natural place to launch the festival.

"There's so much of the diaspora in London," she said. "So many people are represented here. It felt like a full-circle moment for us."

EntertainmentTab.title: Amanda Knox defends Fringe comedy show after claims it will 'trivialise violence'
EntertainmentTab.text:
Amanda Knox, who was convicted and later acquitted of murdering British student Meredith Kercher in Italy in 2007, has defended her solo comedy show following calls for it to be cancelled.

The sold-out show called Cartwheel, which Knox will perform at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, discusses motherhood and how she will explain the case to her daughter.

Knox told the BBC she is not the first person to use comedy to talk about traumatic events and said her material focuses on "how the world is unsafe and unfair towards women".

But Stephanie Kercher, the victim's sister, said she is concerned it will "normalise and trivialise" violence against women, and Meredith, in particular.

Speaking on BBC Breakfast, Stephanie Kercher, said: "What I would say [to Knox] is to think about the family here, think about her friends and to turn the tables if it was your sister that this had happened to, because I know you have a sister as well."

Responding to the comments, Knox said: "The interesting irony of that is that my daughter is a huge motivation for me doing this show.

"It's about how the world is unsafe and unfair towards women and what it means to raise a daughter in that world, knowing how bad it can be.

"If they [Kercher's family] saw my show, they would recognise that."

A petition against the show, set up by a friend of Meredith, has been signed by nearly 5,000 people.

It states the show disrespects her memory and risks making light of such a harrowing event.

Stephanie Kercher added she did not believe Meredith would find these topics of any comedic value.

She said: "Our family's pain is immense. I can't explain to you how much pain our family have been through, and also we're talking two decades later now, this pain.

"I think that if it was a generic theme, as many comedy shows are, even when they're pushing the boundaries, it would be different.

"Because this is associated with an individual case and individual person, I think that's where the worry lies here for me, because who else is this going to then open up this opportunity for?"

But Knox told BBC Scotland News she does not downplay the seriousness of the case and is respectful in her approach.

"I hope people will honestly engage in my work and recognise the deep heart and sensitivity that I bring to it as I tell a very personal story," she said.

The comedy show is set to run over 11 days in the Gilded Balloon Teviot.

Its title Cartwheel references a story that once claimed Knox did cartwheels in the police station after her British roommate's death.

She said the cartwheel becomes a metaphor throughout the show.

"It is about acknowledging that bad things happen in life which will turn you upside down," Knox said.

"But it's also about not letting that arrest your momentum because the only way you can land on your feet is through those difficult experiences."

Knox added she would love to have an open and honest conversation with Kercher's family but claimed she has never had the opportunity.

"It would be incredible for them to see me for who I really am instead of the idea that was delivered to them by people in bad hands," she said.

Since Meredith Kercher's death, Knox has written two books about her imprisonment and served as an executive producer on the biographical drama The Twisted Tale of Amanda Knox.

Now 39, she is married with two children and lives in Washington state.

Knox, from Seattle, and Kercher, from Surrey, were both exchange students sharing a house in the university town of Perugia.

Alongside her then-boyfriend, Raffaele Sollecito, Knox was arrested on suspicion of murdering Kercher, 21, who was found dead in their house.

Her throat had been cut and she had been sexually assaulted.

Knox was found guilty and spent four years in an Italian prison before she and Sollecito were acquitted through an appeal.

She returned home to the US in 2011.

A retrial in 2014 reinstated Knox and Sollecito's convictions but Italy's top appeals court finally overturned them in 2015.

Ivory Coast-born Rudy Guede served 13 years of a 16-year sentence for Kercher's murder after his fingerprints were found at the scene.

The court ruled he did not act alone but after Knox and Sollecito were acquitted, no other accomplices were convicted.

EntertainmentTab.title: Sian Phillips, 93, to step back from acting after memory issues
EntertainmentTab.text:
One of Wales' most celebrated actresses, Dame Siân Phillips, is stepping back from full-scale stage acting after experiencing memory issues during rehearsals.

The 93-year-old made the decision after struggling to remember her lines while preparing for a recent production, according to The Times.

However, Phillips said she would continue performing in smaller projects, including a production with Michael Sheen's Welsh National Theatre next year.

Her career has spanned more than 80 years across stage, television and film.

Phillips told The Times she decided to stop taking on major stage productions after struggling to remember her lines during rehearsals for Atonement at Chichester Festival Theatre earlier this year.

According to the newspaper, she said she would continue performing in her show It's All Greek and is also due to appear in Samuel Beckett's Rockaby for Michael Sheen's Welsh National Theatre next year.

Born in Betws, near Ammanford, Carmarthenshire, in 1933, Phillips grew up speaking Welsh before learning English by listening to the radio.

She began performing as a child, appearing on Welsh-language radio from the age of 11, before studying at the University of Wales and later winning a scholarship to the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art.

She performed in radio productions such as The Archers and an adaptation of John le Carre's Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy, opposite Sir Alec Guinness.

Before her acting career took off, she worked for BBC Wales as a bilingual announcer and newsreader.

Phillips went on to become one of Britain's most acclaimed actresses, appearing in productions including Doctor Who, Calendar Girls, Dune, and I, Claudius.

She won a Bafta for her portrayal of Livia in the BBC's I, Claudius and received a Tony Award nomination for playing the title role in Marlene.

She was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) in 2000 for services to drama, and then a Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire (DBE) in 2016.

EntertainmentTab.title: 'Put your phone down': K-pop band Cortis weighs in on concert etiquette
EntertainmentTab.text:
Kicking off their global tour in the South Korean city of Incheon, the five members of K-pop boy band Cortis saunter onto stage in casual, streetwear-inspired outfits, exuding an effortlessly cool vibe.

"Put your phone down," one of the members bellows. Piercing screams erupt. A sea of illuminated screens flickers back.

"I told you, put your phone down," he repeats, louder this time.

Some fans do just that, but the packed stadium vibrates harder with cheers as thousands of phones stay in the air.

It's hard to say how serious this theatrical command is.

"Put your phone down" is also the name of Cortis's ongoing concert tour, which started in Incheon on 18 July and will head to cities like New York and Los Angeles before returning to Seoul later this month.

The refrain reflects a message the band has long pushed: that fans should stop watching concerts through six-inch screens and engage with their performances in real life.

It's drawn mixed reactions from their fandom: fan-filmed content is a valuable social currency in K-pop.

Park Ji-yeon, for one, could not bring herself to stop recording Cortis's performances. The 22-year-old had specially rented a new, top-tier smartphone for both days of the Cortis concert just so she could film in the highest quality.

"I was standing right at the front, and I couldn't bring myself to put my phone down because I don't know if I'll ever get this opportunity again," she tells the BBC.

"I usually film concerts because I know a lot of those memories will fade as soon as I leave the venue."

While fans like Park continued to film, some heeded the band's call. Kim Ga-eun, 25, who was seated in the amphitheatre-style venue, saw it all.

"People in the back of the standing section were having a great time dancing together. I thought that really reflected the intention behind the concert," she says.

Cortis has had a whirlwind year since debuting last year under record label BigHit Music - part of the company that created pop sensation BTS. Most of its members are teenagers. The oldest of the group, James, is just 20 years old.

Their music videos have each amassed millions of views. Over the weekend they performed at Lollapalooza, the famed music festival in Chicago.

The band's name, Cortis, is derived from the phrase "colour outside the lines", which according to their record label is meant to encapsulate the band's free spirit and refusal to conform to societal rules - which, in this case, appears to include telling fans to resist the temptation of the phone camera.

They join a prominent wave of artists around the world who have been advocating the same.

Singers like Phoebe Bridgers and Alicia Keys have required their concert attendees to use lock pouches - sealed bags that allow people to hold on to their phones without being able to access them.

EntertainmentTab.title: Self Esteem to star in upcoming film Mountain set in 1980s Wales
EntertainmentTab.text:
Singer Self Esteem has landed her first major movie role, starring in a film set in 1980s Wales.

The coming of age story, Mountain, directed by Celyn Jones, was filmed in his home town of Holyhead, on Anglesey.

Peter Mullan, Iwan Rheon and Seth Isaac Thomas will star alongside Rebecca Lucy Taylor, who goes by the stage name Self Esteem.

The film tells the story of a neglected young boy in 1980s Wales, looking for friendship and community when he meets a man living alone on a mountain.

Jones said filming the project, which wrapped earlier this year, had been "an emotional and spiritual homecoming".

Self Esteem, known for her hit tracks Focus Is Power and I Do This All The Time, is no stranger to commanding both the stage and screen.

The pop star performed in the hit London West End musical, Cabaret in 2023, and the revival of David Hare's 1975 play, Teeth 'n' Smiles, earlier this year.

She also took on roles in the Sky Comedy series Smothered and Sky TV drama I Hate Suzie.

EntertainmentTab.title: Nadia Sawalha threatens legal action against ITV over Loose Women removal
EntertainmentTab.text:
Loose Women panellist Nadia Sawalha has threatened to take legal action against ITV, claiming the network dropped her for speaking out in support of Palestinian rights.

A legal organisation representing her has sent a pre-action letter to ITV, claiming the broadcaster "subjected Nadia to direct discrimination, indirect discrimination and harassment because of her protected philosophical beliefs".

In an Instagram video, external, Sawalha said she had become "the target of an escalating campaign of smears, complaints, hostile media coverage and targeted calls to have me removed from Loose Women".

She added: "Since then, ITV have taken me on and off Loose Women a number of times." BBC News has asked ITV for comment.

The presenter said she "began speaking publicly in support of Palestine in December 2023", two months after the 7 October Hamas attacks on Israel and Israel's subsequent military campaign in Gaza.

She said she was "speaking out against brutal oppression", but her critics have accused her of promoting false claims and conspiracies about Israel and Jewish people.

A group of Jewish executives in the entertainment industry recently sent a dossier to ITV, urging the channel not to reinstate her, citing what they called "repeated examples of conspiratorial rhetoric, inflammatory commentary, disinformation, and antisemitic discourse".

Sawalha said she hadn't had a chance to see the document and answer the accusations, but has denied antisemitism.

Two newspapers that previously accused Sawalha and her husband of antisemitism and supporting terrorism have since issued apologies and paid damages, external to the couple.

In her video on Thursday, Sawalha said she had "mostly been told" by ITV that "the reason for [my removal] was, and I quote, 'It's all a bit noisy out there for us'."

EntertainmentTab.title: Stephen Bear jailed for Georgia Harrison restraining order breach
EntertainmentTab.text:
Reality TV contestant Stephen Bear is back in prison after admitting breaching a restraining order that banned him from posting online about ex-partner Georgia Harrison.

The order was imposed when Bear was jailed in 2023 after he filmed and shared a video of the pair having sex on OnlyFans and WhatsApp without Harrison's knowledge.

The 36-year-old was told not to post or incite comments on social media about that case or Harrison but did so multiple times in 2025 while she was pregnant.

In a statement read to Chelmsford Crown Court, the Love Island star and campaigner said Bear's online presence left her "feeling petrified" and she feared for her safety. He was jailed for 16 months.

Bear, of Walthamstow, east London, admitted the charge of harassment – breaching of a restraining order, at a previous hearing in June.

Judge Christopher Morgan, who presided over the original trial in 2023, said Bear's posts and videos in 2025 were "to ensure the maximum harm [was] caused to Georgia Harrison".

"You knew all of that was untrue, and yet you posted it," he said.

"You left Miss Harrison, I'm afraid, at the mercy of any individual who had aligned themselves with your lies."

In addition to the prison sentence, the judge extended the restraining order to stop Bear from contacting Harrison's mother and her friend, which remains in place until a new order is imposed.

After serving half his original sentence, Bear was released from prison, but between 1 March 2025 and 21 July 2025 began posting on Instagram, TikTok, X, YouTube and Facebook about the case and Harrison.

The court heard these were "consistently posted messages of the most abhorrent and harmful type".

Addressing Bear, the judge said: "What you did in that three to four-month period is simply victim-blaming."

Harrison did not attend court, but the prosecution read out a statement in which she described feeling isolated, exposed and unsafe, and asked for the restraining order to be extended.

She said the significant stress had made her worry about her unborn child and caused her to "spiral" on some occasions.

"I shut him out of my mind for a long time and it's not fair that he's managed to crawl his way back in," she said.

Bear arrived for Thursday's sentencing with his wife, who is eight months pregnant.

As he walked in to court, he refused to answer questions but gave a thumbs-up and said: "Wish me luck guys. See you soon, hopefully."

As his barrister spoke about why there should be a reduced sentence, Bear appeared to briefly cry.

He shook his head as he was taken away to begin another prison term.

EntertainmentTab.title: TikTok star Sydney Towle, who shared her cancer journey online, dies aged 26
EntertainmentTab.text:
Sydney Towle, a popular social media influencer who shared her experience living with a rare, aggressive form of cancer, has died at the age of 26.

Towle's family announced her death, from complications related to bile duct cancer that had spread to other parts of her body, on her social media accounts on Thursday.

"Syd went peacefully last night after an almost three-year-long battle with cholangiocarcinoma," her brother Austin said in a video message, alongside their mother, on TikTok.

Towle, who was moved to hospice care earlier this week, had over a million followers on TikTok and over 200,000 on Instagram.

She spent the last three years chronicling her daily life as a young person going through chemotherapy and living with cancer, with all its hopes, joys and struggles. She had been living in New York City at the time of her death.

"We are so proud of how hard Sydney fought and for sharing her journey with so many people," Towle's family said in a statement.

"She wanted to raise awareness for rare cancers and was passionate about promoting self-advocacy. We will continue her legacy and honour her in every way we can."

Following the announcement of her death, thousands of followers posted messages on Towle's social media accounts paying tribute to her and sending well wishes to her family.

"Sweet angel. Fly high," actress Alyssa Milano commented. "Praying for all who loved her. She is really something special."

"You were such a bright light and will be missed," one person wrote on Instagram, while another said: "How lucky we all are to have found you on the internet. Thank you for sharing yourself and your story."

In May, Towle posted a series of videos from the hospital where she was receiving treatment for complications related to her cancer.

She shared that her cancer had spread to her peritoneum, a membrane that lines the abdominal and pelvic cavities and protects internal organs.

On 19 May, she posted a video of herself, sitting beside her mother in the hospital, in which she said her oncologist had told her he would no longer treat her cancer, recommending she begin end-of-life care. Towle said she would not accept this and vowed to continue fighting, choosing instead to switch to another specialist.

Despite her illness, she expressed fervent optimism and joy for life on her social media accounts. She often posted videos of herself dancing, getting ready, and having fun with friends.

She recently fulfilled her dream of modelling, walking in a swimsuit for The Chemo Club x Post Swim show at Miami Swim Week.

"Rich in life because my friends choose to spend a Saturday fundraising for cancer research," Towle wrote in a post in March.

"Go get a pint of Ben and Jerry's, watch your favourite movie, remember that life is good and bad things happen sometimes but that doesn't make it a bad life," Towle wrote in another post last year.

Towle was not shy about showing her stomach, where she had a hepatic artery pump implanted, on social media.

"I have only recently started seeing the resilience and beauty in this body," she wrote in a post last year, alongside photos of herself in a swimsuit. "Scars that remind me of how far I've come. And I'm reminded that dreams only end when you allow them to."

GeneralTab.title: Burnham to set out cost-of-living measures as he tours UK
GeneralTab.text:
The prime minister is set to announce "a series of measures to make life easier" for those struggling with the cost of living in the coming days, Downing Street says.

No 10 says Andy Burnham's plans are to "give people some room to breathe". He will also focus on ways of "improving high streets" as he embarks on a tour of the UK.

But the government is facing continued pressure over its early release scheme for prisoners in England and Wales – with criticism of the fact that two of PC Andrew Harper's killers will be eligible from next year.

Burnham is also likely to face pressure for more action on the cost of living – although significant interventions are unlikely before October's Budget.

Even then, Chancellor John Healey has made it clear he will oversee "strong fiscal discipline" – which will limit how much the government has to spend.

The prime minister has been on holiday this week, but Downing Street said he would be in "listening mode" in the coming days as he tours the UK's nations and regions and works on a "10-year plan to bring back hope".

A spokesman for the prime minister said: "He thinks Westminster has got used to telling people that everyday hassles – like hidden pricing and consumers being ripped off – must be accepted as part of life.

"He doesn't think that's right. That's why he's going to start rolling out a series of pro-consumer cost of living measures to give people some room to breathe."

The spokesman added: "He's also going to be kicking off his summer tour around the country, getting out of Westminster and meeting people where they are.

"The prime minister is going to be in listening mode to help inform his 10-year plan to bring back hope and make Britain better off."

There are, though, likely to be continued questions about the forthcoming early release scheme, due to start in October.

One of Burnham's first acts in Downing Street was to order a review which limited the range of people who would be eligible.

But those convicted of manslaughter will still qualify for the scheme – including two of the killers of PC Andrew Harper.

The prime minister has faced calls from PC Harper's family, former senior police officers and opposition politicians for them to be denied early release.

But he has said he cannot go any further without risking prison capacity. Downing Street said on Saturday night that position remained unchanged, despite reports the prime minister could revisit the case.

The Conservatives said the government's "tax hikes and red tape are hammering our high streets".

Shadow chancellor Mel Stride said: "This is breathtaking hypocrisy from Burnham… they are forcing businesses to close, destroying jobs and driving up prices for the public.

"Meanwhile, Labour are plotting to release dangerous criminals onto our streets, leaving people feeling unsafe in their communities."

Liberal Democrat Treasury spokeswoman Daisy Cooper said struggling high street businesses "need more than a new PM embarking on a vanity tour this summer".

She said the PM should adopt the Lib Dem plan for high streets: "That means reversing the damaging jobs tax, delivering an emergency VAT cut for hospitality, replacing broken business rates and cracking down on the ghost landlords leaving our shop fronts vacant."

Reform UK's economic spokesman Robert Jenrick said: "If Andy Burnham wants to help people with the cost of living, he should scrap the green levies and taxes on energy bills and rule out tax rises at the Budget."

GeneralTab.title: Gianni Infantino: Fifa criticises campaign to oust president
GeneralTab.text:
Fifa has strongly criticised what it calls a "concerted and ongoing effort" to "undermine" the organisation and its president Gianni Infantino.

The statement follows a Daily Telegraph report, external which claimed Infantino's alleged lover was given a severance payment by Uefa after he had an affair while he was its general secretary.

A Fifa spokesperson told the Telegraph Infantino "strongly denies" the allegations and that they are "categorically untrue".

Fifa has now itself hit out at "unsubstantiated assertions and demonstrably false claims", adding that "speculation and insinuation should not be presented as fact".

Infantino has come under increasing pressure from Uefa and European football associations over his aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal.

FFE would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights, with 21% sold off to a private investment company.

Uefa has said it has lost confidence in Infantino, while Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) president Lise Klaveness on Friday called on the Swiss-Italian to resign.

European football's governing body says its threat to boycott Fifa events remains on the table, adding that assurances the FFE plan could not be revived have not been received.

"The Fifa president was democratically elected by Fifa's Member Associations and continues to serve with their mandate," Fifa said in its statement on Saturday.

"It is increasingly evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine Fifa and its president.

"Those who do not have the support of Fifa's member associations should not seek to achieve through allegation, insinuation or misinformation what they cannot achieve through Fifa's established democratic processes."

Opposition to Infantino is largely from within Europe.

The Mexican Football Federation broke ranks with its regional governing body Concacaf to come out in support of Infantino.

It echoed a statement from Conmebol - South America's governing body - in saying it would reject any attempt to remove Infantino without a vote involving all 211 Fifa member countries.

Infantino is also unanimously backed by the 54 nations of the Confederation of African Football (Caf).

GeneralTab.title: Why PC Andrew Harper's death touched so many
GeneralTab.text:
On the night of 15 August 2019, Lissie Harper got a knock at the door. She thought it was her husband Andrew coming home from work.

Instead, it was uniformed officers, there to tell her that the man she had married four weeks earlier had been killed while on police duty.

"Everything I had known in my life to be true was robbed away. Every ounce of beautiful peace, gone," Lissie later said of the moment she was told.

They had met as teenagers and were together for 13 years.

In her eulogy at his funeral, Lissie recalled how Andrew would pass her notes in class.

They were, she said, "true childhood sweethearts, loving one another more and more with each passing day".

They had been about to go on their honeymoon.

But, on that night nearly seven years ago, everything changed.

The case has been back in the headlines because two of PC Harper's killers – Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole – will become eligible to be released early under government plans to tackle prison overcrowding.

As the disturbing details of the case are revisited, his family, fellow officers and the public are outraged once more – at what happened, and at the perpetrators' impending release.

PC Harper's death was brutal and devastating, causing shock, anger and an outpouring of grief across the country.

Pictures of the smiling faces of his teenage killers laughing and joking as they left court only added to that anger.

PC Harper had been about to head home at the end of a long shift when he and a colleague were called to reports of a burglary.

He was "going beyond the call of duty", the prosecutor at the Old Bailey trial in 2020 said.

During the case, haunting dashcam footage from the police patrol car was played showing the moment PC Harper confronted teenagers Henry Long, Bowers and Cole down a dark country lane. He then disappeared from view.

His ankles had got caught in a strap trailing behind the car being driven by Long that had been used to tow a stolen quad bike.

PC Harper was dragged for over a mile. He died on the road. His police badge and stab vest were found scattered along the route.

The three teenagers were tried for murder. In the end, the jury convicted Bowers and Cole of manslaughter. Long had already pleaded guilty to that offence.

It meant the jury was not sure that PC Harper's killers knew they were dragging the officer behind the car.

But the Judge, Mr Justice Edis, described it as a manslaughter case which was "very close to a case of murder" in its seriousness.
